## Today is different

- Last week you told me you wanted **less revision** and **more hands-on work**.
- Today we're skipping straight to Stata.
- The whole lecture is a three-part activity — one for each type of bivariate analysis.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## But first: why does any of this matter?

- Some of you have felt like you're learning **mechanical tasks without knowing why**.
- That's a fair observation — and it's worth addressing directly.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The building blocks aren't obvious yet

- Generating a histogram or tabulating a single variable can feel pointless.
- But these are the **building blocks** of independent empirical analysis.
- Right now you're learning to use a tool. Later, you'll decide what to do with it.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## What you're building toward

- **Problem Set 2** asks you to analyse a dataset of your choice, with variables of your choice.
- You will need to identify the right tool for the right pair of variables — and execute it.
- Everything you've done so far is preparation for that.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## The do files are templates

- The do files in our shared folder aren't just course materials — they're **starting points for your own analysis**.
- You've set up an identical folder structure on your computer for exactly this reason.
- Download a do file, update the working directory, and you have a working template.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## What happens when you run a do file top to bottom

- Stata executes every line in sequence.
- Plots appear because the do file contains graph commands.
- This isn't magic — it's a **reproducible record** of your analysis.
- Today we'll use a new do file as a template: ``bivariate-lecture.do``

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Three cases, three parts

::: nonincremental

| Case | Variable 1 | Variable 2 | Tools                                 |
|------|------------|------------|---------------------------------------|
| 1    | Nominal    | Nominal    | Cross-tabulation, bivariate bar chart |
| 2    | Nominal    | Numeric    | Compare means, bar chart of means     |
| 3    | Numeric    | Numeric    | Scatterplot, regression line          |

:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Case 1: Nominal + Nominal

- **Tools:** Cross-tabulation and bivariate bar chart.
- Open ``bivariate-lecture.do`` and go to **Case 1**.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Case 1 example: Gender and vote choice

::: nonincremental

- ``tabulate b02 y09, column nofreq``
- ``graph hbar (count), over(y09) over(b02) asyvars``

:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Case 1: Your turn

::: nonincremental

- **Variables:** Gender (``y09``) and interest in politics (``a03``).
- Clean ``a03``: ``replace a03 = . if a03 < 0``
- Create a cross-tabulation and a bivariate chart.
- Use the gender/vote choice commands as templates.

:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Case 2: Nominal + Numeric

- **Tools:** Compare means and bar chart of means.
- Open ``bivariate-lecture.do`` and go to **Case 2**.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Case 2 example: Newspaper readership and ideology

::: nonincremental

- ``sort k03``
- ``by k03: summarize e01``
- ``graph hbar e01, over(k03)``

:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Case 2: Your turn

::: nonincremental

- **Variables:** Socio-economic class (``sc``) and ideology (``e01``).
- Does ideology differ across socio-economic classes?
- Use the newspaper/ideology commands as a template — just swap the variables.

:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Case 3: Numeric + Numeric

- **Tools:** Scatterplot and regression line.
- Open ``bivariate-lecture.do`` and go to **Case 3**.
- This case uses the **Brexit Regional dataset**.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Case 3 example: Import shock and Brexit

::: nonincremental

- ``twoway (scatter leave_share import_shock) (lfit leave_share import_shock)``

:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Case 3: Your turn

::: nonincremental

- **Variables:** Share with higher education (``share_high_skill``) and Leave vote share (``leave_share``).
- Do regions with more graduates vote differently on Brexit?
- Use the import shock commands as a template — just swap ``import_shock`` for ``share_high_skill``.

:::

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Why this matters

- Choosing the right tool depends on knowing your variable types.
- The do files you've been working with are templates for PS2.
- Every analysis you'll do in this module starts with the question: **what types are my variables?**
